implementation_notes: Scala expresses the pattern directly: `lazy val image: Image = Image.load(path)` evaluates its right-hand side the first time the value is accessed, and Scala 3 implements SIP-20 so the initialization is at most once and thread-safe without holding the enclosing object's monitor for the whole construction. A single deferred member therefore needs no stand-in class at all; the explicit proxy is still justified when the subject must be built with different parameters per access, when it must be replaceable, or when callers need to ask whether it was initialized (a lazy val cannot tell you).
pitfalls: Recursive lazy vals are undefined: a lazy val whose initializer touches itself may deadlock, and the docs flag the behaviour as unsupported rather than an error.

Scala 2.13 and earlier compile each lazy val with a monitor on the enclosing instance, so several lazy vals in one object initialize sequentially and can deadlock against unrelated synchronized code (Scala 3's SIP-20 scheme removed that external lock).
A lazy val pays a state check on every access and is still per-instance; a lazy val in a companion object is initialized once for the whole process, not once per object.
